title: Guy Lakan
text:
About

I completed my PhD in Finance at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and am currently a Postdoctoral Fellow in the Finance Department at the Kellogg School of Management, Northwestern University. My research focuses on institutional investors and alternative investments, with particular interest in how investors make investment decisions and how regulation shapes capital allocation. I also study household financial decision-making, including how financial literacy and bargaining affect the costs and outcomes of long-term saving.

title: Policy & Media
text:
Israel Knesset, Finance Committee | 2026
Invited to present research during the Knesset’s deliberations on a proposed amendment to the tax treatment of pension and provident funds. I discussed how tax uncertainty can distort institutional investors’ portfolio allocation, discourage direct investment in real estate and infrastructure, and shift capital toward foreign assets.



Israel Knesset, Economic Affairs Committee | 2023
Presented research on the evolution of Israeli institutional investors’ exposure to the technology sector before the Knesset Subcommittee for the Promotion of the High-Tech Industry. The discussion focused on whether domestic institutional capital could help offset the decline in foreign investment and on the effectiveness of government programs designed to encourage institutional investment in Israeli technology.

SELECTED COMMENTARY

The Capital Market Authority Asked Institutional Investors to Intervene. Now It Is Investigating Them for Doing So
TheMarker | 2026
On the tension between institutional investor activism and regulatory definitions of control, and the risk that regulatory uncertainty may discourage institutional investors from actively monitoring public companies.


An Important Reform, but Not Enough: Barriers to Institutional Investment in Infrastructure and Real Estate Remain
Calcalist | 2025 | With Moshe Bareket
On how tax uncertainty can discourage pension and provident funds from investing directly in real estate and infrastructure, even when such investments are economically attractive and widely used by institutional investors abroad.


Treating the Symptom, Not the Disease: Israel’s Dollar Liquidity Risk Is Structural
Calcalist | 2025
On the systemic liquidity risks created by the growing foreign exposure of Israeli institutional investors and the use of derivatives, and why the appropriate policy response should address market-wide liquidity rather than impose additional liquidity requirements on individual institutions.


Where Is the Regulator? Wealth Transfers Between Pension Savers
TheMarker | 2025
On how stale valuations of illiquid assets can create transfers between savers who move across pension products or investment tracks, and why the growth of alternative investments requires a reconsideration of existing valuation practices.


Can a Pension Scandal Undermine Trust in the Retirement System?
Calcalist | 2024
On the broader implications of the Slice pension scandal for public confidence in Israel’s long-term savings system and the role of regulation, distribution channels, and financial advice in maintaining trust.

RESEARCH IN THE PUBLIC SPHERE

Private Equity and Venture Capital Fund Performance: Evidence from a Large Sample of Israeli Limited Partners
Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance | 2023
With Alon Brav and Yishay Yafeh
A discussion of our research on the private-market investments of Israeli institutional investors, including their access to private funds, performance in local versus foreign investments, and the limitations of commonly used commercial private-market databases.

With Alon Brav and Yishay Yafeh
Honourable Mention, ICPM 2025 Research Award Finalist
Using detailed investment-committee discussions together with long-run cash-flow data, this paper studies how institutional investors evaluate and select private-market funds. We examine the information used in committee deliberations, how decision-making differs across private equity, venture capital, real estate, infrastructure, and private debt, and how these discussions relate to subsequent investment outcomes.



Job Market Paper
This paper examines differences in the management fees paid by minority and non-minority savers in long-term savings products. Combining reduced-form evidence with a structural model of fee bargaining, the paper studies how differences in bargaining behavior and bargaining costs can generate persistent disparities in the fees paid by otherwise comparable savers.



With Itay Kedmi
This paper studies an investor-side regulation that required institutional investors to acquire independent information before investing in corporate bonds. We show that the mandate changed institutional investors’ participation in public debt markets, increased concentration in their bond positions, and shifted credit toward private lending. The effects are strongest for information-sensitive issuers, with important consequences for firms’ access to public debt markets.



This paper studies how the valuation of illiquid alternative assets affects transfers between savers in long-term savings products. Because private assets are valued infrequently, their reported values can lag changes in economic conditions. Using the COVID-19 shock, the paper examines how stale valuations can generate wealth transfers between investors who enter, exit, or switch savings products at different points in time.

WORK IN PROGRESS

Trading Across the Capital Structure: Information and Institutional Investor Behavior
I study how information shapes the timing of institutional investors’ trading across equity and corporate bond markets. By tracing portfolio adjustments in both the stocks and bonds of the same firms, I examine whether institutional investors trade first in one market and subsequently adjust their positions in the other, and how these patterns vary with the information environment. The project uses cross-market trading and timing to shed light on how information is incorporated into institutional portfolio decisions across the capital structure.


Information Frictions and Matching in Private Capital Markets
I study how information frictions shape the matching process between institutional investors and private fund managers. When a fund is farther from an investor, direct information about the fund and its manager is more limited, making the investment decisions of other institutional investors potentially more informative. I examine whether an institutional investor is more likely to commit to a fund after nearby investors have done so, and whether this dependence becomes stronger as the fund is located farther away. The project sheds light on how learning from other investors affects the formation of LP–GP relationships when information is scarce.
